theme: God speaks from the whirlwind, “Where were you?”
readingInstruction: Read Job 38:1-39:30. Slow down. God has not spoken in the book since the prologue. Read his questions aloud and try to answer them honestly. You will find that you cannot.
settingTheScene: After thirty-seven chapters of human speeches, God answers. He comes in a storm, the sort of storm Elihu was describing at the end of his speech. He does not explain Job’s suffering. He does not mention the court scene in heaven, or Satan, or the test. He does not defend himself or scold Job. He asks Job a series of questions about the world he has made, and the questions are so large that Job’s own question seems to shrink. This is the turning point of the book.
observation: “Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind” (38:1).
“Who is this that darkens counsel by words without knowledge?” (38:2).
“Dress for action like a man; I will question you, and you make it known to me” (38:3).
“Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth? Tell me, if you have understanding” (38:4).
“When the morning stars sang together and all the sons of God shouted for joy” (38:7).
God shut the sea behind doors and said, “Thus far shall you come, and no farther, and here shall your proud waves be stayed” (38:8-11).
“Have you entered into the springs of the sea…Have the gates of death been revealed to you?” (38:16-17).
God asks about light, snow, hail, rain, the constellations, and the clouds (38:19-38).
“Who provides for the raven its prey, when its young ones cry to God for help?” (38:41).
Chapter 39 moves through wild animals: the mountain goat, the wild donkey, the wild ox, the ostrich, the war horse, the hawk, and the eagle.
interpretation:
The first thing to notice is what God does not say. He gives no reason for Job’s suffering. If Job had wanted a theological explanation, he does not receive one. Some readers are disappointed. But think about what has happened. Job has been asking for an audience with God for thirty chapters. Now he has it. And what he receives is not an argument. It is a presence.

The second thing is that God’s questions are pitched at the right size. Job has been treating the world as if it should make sense to him, as if God owed him an account. The questions say: do you know how the world works? Where were you when it began? Do you know how to feed the lion, or when the mountain goats give birth? The point is not to humiliate Job. It is to show him that he is in the middle of a world far larger and wiser than he can see. If he cannot understand the sea, how can he understand the plan of God?

Pay attention to the tenderness behind the questions. The sea is shut in with doors, like a newborn wrapped in swaddling clothes (38:9). The morning stars sing at creation. The raven’s young cry out, and God provides. The wild donkey is given the wilderness as a home, and the ostrich is allowed to be foolish, because he made her that way. This is not a cold, mechanical universe. It is full of joy and wildness and care. It is the work of a God who delights in what he has made.

This is, in a way, the answer to Job’s question. Job wanted to know whether God is just. God’s answer is to show him God’s wisdom and God’s care in a thousand other places, and to invite Job to trust that this wisdom extends to the part of the world he cannot understand: his own suffering.

The answer to suffering is not an explanation. It is the character of the one who rules.
connection: Psalm 104 is a hymn that follows the same path as God’s speech. Jesus used the birds and flowers to say that the Father cares for his children: “Look at the birds of the air…your heavenly Father feeds them” (Matthew 6:26). Colossians 1:16-17 says that all things were created through the Son, and in him all things hold together.
application:
Go outside and spend ten minutes looking carefully at something God made: an insect, a tree, a cloud. Ask God to teach you something about himself from it.

When you are tempted to demand that God explain himself, return to chapter 38 and answer the questions honestly.

Pray that you would trust God’s character even when you cannot see his plan.
prayerPrompts: Praise God for something he has made that you did not.
Tell him that you are small and that you trust him because of who he is.
Ask him to help you delight in what he has made.
